# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 161)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber. Little Rawdon sent to school; Rawdon visited him shortly after and found him well and happy.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph. Great George on throne; ladies wore gigots and tortoise-shell combs. Later seasonal details: Rain threatened since morning but held off; bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs; bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; children chased hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; Bryngate (Tassa Brackwood departed); Yarlton (Tassa settled; Colan Lindson followed within month); London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House, Gaunt Square, Serpentine, Cursitor Street); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Mirecombe; Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe; Fenmere; school in City; Astley's; May Fair; Chancery Lane; the Temple.

## Rebecca's Ascendant Period and Deterioration (Chapters 21–22)

**Social Triumphs**: Court presentation, Gaunt House musical triumph, diplomatic circles including French Embassy and Prince of Peterwaradin, exclusive supper placement, elaborate charades entertainment.

**Contempt for Rawdon and Growing Isolation**: Dismisses him patronizingly: "Do what you like--dine where you please--go and have ginger-beer and sawdust at Astley's, or psalm-singing with Lady Jane--only don't expect me to busy myself with the boy." Claims credit for his social position. Nobody wants Rawdon at parties; she is often asked without him. Looks upon him as errand-man and humble slave, did not care or miss him or anybody.

**Steyne's Financial Schemes and Investigations (Chapter 22)**
- Previously gave Becky money to pay off debt to Briggs; suspected she misappropriated funds but too delicate to confront her.
- **Investigation of Briggs**: Steyne orchestrated "pumping" of Miss Briggs through Mr. Fiche (his confidential servant), who monitored Crawleys' livery arrangements. Extracted truth: Briggs received only black silk gown, nothing else.
- **Truth of Situation**: Rebecca told Steyne false narrative claiming she paid Briggs £1,125 and detailed securities invested. Steyne laughed privately, suspected her scheming, made no additional proposals.
- **Briggs's Actual Position**: Left legacy by Miss Crawley; relatives took part; Colonel Crawley invested £600+ of her money with "best security and interest"; Sir Pitt promised to invest remainder. Briggs begged Steyne never tell Rawdon of her confessions, fearing demand for repayment.
- **Steyne's Offer to Briggs**: Offered her position at his Hall; Briggs stipulated only that little Rawdon visit her there. Rebecca promised anything and joyfully reported to Rawdon, who was relieved weight lifted from conscience.

**Emerging Concerns About Rebecca's Conduct**
- **Rawdon's Observation**: Told young Southdown of Steyne's bounty; Southdown eyed Crawley with surprising air.
- **Lady Jane and Sir Pitt's Alarm**: Both looked "odd and alarmed" upon hearing of Steyne's bounties. Insisted Rawdon must accompany her everywhere; suggested placing Queen's Crawley girl with her as companion.
- **Sir Pitt's Direct Confrontation**: Expostulated with Rebecca about dismissal of Briggs and other delicate matters. She pointed out necessity of Steyne's protection. Had something very like quarrel with once-admired Becky. Spoke of family honour, Crawley reputation; expressed indignation at her receiving young Frenchmen (Messieurs de Truffigny and Champignac), Lord Steyne himself (whose carriage always at her door, passed hours daily in her company). As head of house, implored her to be prudent. Society already speaking lightly of her. Lord Steyne, though greatest station and talents, a man whose attentions would compromise any woman.
- **Becky's Promises and Steyne's Continued Visits**: Becky promised anything and everything Pitt wanted; but Lord Steyne came to her house as often as ever, and Sir Pitt's anger increased.
- **Lady Jane's Response**: Ambiguous whether angry or pleased that Pitt at last found fault with Rebecca. For refusing all further intercourse with Steyne and declining charades invitation; but Sir Pitt thought acceptance necessary as Royal Highness would be there. At charades party, both Pitts quit early. Becky hardly spoke to Pitt or noticed Lady Jane. Pitt declared her behaviour monstrously indecorous, reprobated play-acting and fancy dressing as highly unbecoming a British female, and after charades took brother Rawdon severely to task for appearing himself and allowing his wife to join in such improper exhibitions.

## Amelia's Separation and Maternal Anguish (Chapter 22)

**George's Permanent Separation**: Departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated; mother's heart breaking. Now visits on pony with coachman. Completely unaffected by separation; adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner" within two days. **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Daily Ritual of Longing**: On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk to Russell Square; rests by garden railing opposite Osborne house. Looks up at illuminated drawing-room windows; at nine o'clock sees chamber where Georgy sleeps. Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired.

**Church Encounter**: One Sunday, saw George and Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite, followed to Foundling Church where she sat to see boy's head. George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears.

**Physical Decline**: Grows care-worn and sad. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights. Kissed father, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before departure.

**Letter to Jos (Chapter 21)**: Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support from parents (unaware Jos's annuity continues but money-lender receives it; Sedley sold it for capital).

## Little Rawdon at School (Chapter 22)

**Departure**: Honest Briggs made up little kit. Rebecca would not let Rawdon have carriage; cab brought instead. Rebecca did not offer kiss when he left; child did not propose to embrace her. Walked home very dismally; dined alone with Briggs. Very kind to her, grateful for love and watchfulness. Conscience smote him about borrowing Briggs's money and aiding deception.

**Boy's School Experience**: Young Blackball constituted little Rawdon his fag, shoe-black, and breakfast toaster; initiated him into Latin Grammar; thrashed him three or four times, not severely. Got beating deemed good for him; blacking shoes, toasting bread, fagging deemed necessary parts of young English gentleman's education.

**Rawdon's Visit**: Found lad sufficiently well and happy, grinning and laughing in little black gown and breeches.

## Rawdon's Financial Crisis and Spunging-House (Chapter 22)

**Arrest and Detention**: Rawdon drove to Mr. Moss's mansion in Cursitor Street, Chancery Lane, and was duly inducted into that dismal place of hospitality. Morning was breaking over house-tops as rattling cab woke echoes there. A little pink-eyed Jew-boy let the party in. Rawdon welcomed to ground-floor apartments by Mr. Moss, who cheerfully asked if he would like something warm after his drive.

**Prior History**: Colonel had been lodger at Mr. Moss's establishment once or twice before. On first visit as bachelor, liberated by generosity of his aunt. On second mishap, little Becky, with greatest spirit and kindness, borrowed sum from Lord Southdown and coaxed her husband's creditor (who was her shawl, velvet-gown, lace pocket-handkerchief, trinket, and gim-crack purveyor) to take portion of sum claimed and Rawdon's promissory note for remainder. On both occasions capture and release conducted with utmost gallantry on all sides; Moss and Colonel on very best of terms.

**Current Predicament**: Colonel not so depressed as some mortals would be quitting palace and placens uxor, finding themselves barred into spunging-house; had been lodger here before. Reader may be assured such trivial domestic incidents can't unfrequently occur in life of man who lives on nothing a year.

**Mr. Moss's Hospitality**: Offered Colonel his old bed, everything comfortable, kept aired by best of company. Recently slept in by Honorable Captain Famish, of Fiftieth Dragoons, whose Ma took him out after fortnight to punish him, but he punished champagne and had party every night—tip-top swells from clubs and West End, including Captain Ragg, Honorable Deuceace (Temple resident), and gentlemen who know good wine. Moss has Doctor of Divinity upstairs, five gents in coffee-room, and Mrs. Moss has table-d'hôte at half-past five with cards or music afterwards.

**Rawdon's Letter from Spunging-House**: Called for pens, ink, paper. Miss Moss (dark-eyed damsel, sat on breakfast table edge displaying stocking drapery and ex-white satin shoe down at heel) brought paper between her own finger and thumb. Letter states: Nathan's debt one-hundred-fifty, with costs one-hundred-seventy. Asks Rebecca to send desk and clothes—he's in pumps and white tie ("something like Miss M's stockings")—he has seventy in desk. Instructs her to drive to Nathan's—offer seventy-five down and ask him to renew—say he'll take wine—may as well have dinner sherry but not pictures, too dear. If Nathan won't stand it, take his ticker and spare things to Balls—must have sum tonight. Won't do to let it stand over, tomorrow's Sunday; beds here not very clean; there may be other things out against him. Glad it isn't Rawdon's Saturday for coming home. God bless you.

**Waiting for Rescue**: Letter sealed with wafer, dispatched by messenger always hanging about Mr. Moss's establishment. Rawdon, having seen messenger depart, went into courtyard and smoked cigar with tolerably easy mind—in spite of bars overhead—for Mr. Moss's courtyard railed in like cage, lest gentlemen boarding with him take fancy to escape. Calculated three hours utmost time required before Becky should arrive and open his prison doors. Passed these pretty cheerfully smoking, reading paper, and in coffee-room with acquaintance Captain Walker, with whom he cut for sixpences for some hours with pretty equal luck on either side.

## Key Relationships (Chapter 22)

**Rawdon and Rebecca's Estrangement**: Estrangement more than he knew or acknowledged. She did not care; did not miss him. Looked upon him as errand-man and humble slave.

**Rawdon and Lady Jane**: Very fond of young Rawdon, as was her little girl. Rawdon thankful for fondness. Best and honestest feelings of man came out in paternal feeling in their presence. Secured kindness and sincere regard.

## Minor Characters
- **Mr. Moss**: Proprietor of spunging-house on Cursitor Street; on very best of terms with Colonel
- **Miss Moss**: Dark-eyed damsel at establishment, grown very fat, stockings down at heel
- **Captain Walker**: Acquaintance of Rawdon at Moss's
- **Captain Famish**: Recent guest at Mr. Moss's, Fifth Dragoons
- **Mrs. Moss**: Hosts table-d'hôte at half-past five
- **Nathan**: Money-lender; creditor for one-hundred-fifty debt (with costs one-hundred-seventy)
- **Briggs, Old Mr. Osborne, Miss Osborne, Old Mr. Sedley, Mr. Wenham, Mr. Fiche, Messieurs de Truffigny and Champignac, Duc de la Jabotiere, Tassa Brackwood**: As previously documented
